How to Collect Data?

Observe
  • you see what you see
  • not all things can be observed
  • good for ‘who, what, when and where’ questions
Ask
  • potentially, can ask about anything
  • responses may not be accurate
    • unwilling
    • unable
    • rely on consumer memory
  • good for ‘why’ questions

What Is Observation?

A systematic process of recording patterns of occurrences or behaviors without normally communicating with the people involved.

What Are the Pros and Cons of Observation Over Asking?

Pros of Observe over Ask
  • No communication with the respondent
  • No self-report distortions
  • No need to rely on respondents’ memory
  • Non-verbal behavior data might be collected
  • Certain data might get collected quicker
  • Environmental conditions can be recorded
Cons of Observe over Ask
  • Cognitive phenomena can’t be observed
  • Observer biases: interpretation of the data might be a problem
  • Not all activities can be recorded
  • Possible invasion of privacy
  • Behaviors might change

What Are Qualitative Methods?

  • What shapes a consumer’s choices?
  • Qualitative methods help us understand what cannot be directly observed or easily measured.
    • Feelings, thoughts, intentions, experiences, and motives
  • Consumers may be unable or unwilling to explain some motivations directly in a survey.
    • Example: Interest in a luxury car may partly reflect identity, status, or a sense of achievement.
    • When asked directly, the consumer may instead emphasize practical considerations: “I got a great deal,” “I liked its performance,” or “My old car needed to be replaced.”

Different formats, one purpose: uncover how consumers understand, feel, and decide.

Types of Qualitative Methods: Individual In-Depth Interviews (IDI)

  • Nondirective interviews
    • Begin with broad, open-ended questions and give the participant substantial freedom to guide the response
    • The interviewer must
      • build rapport and create a comfortable environment
      • probe for clarification and detail without suggesting an answer
      • redirect the conversation when it moves away from the research topic
      • ask follow-up questions to uncover the reasons behind a response
  • Semi-structured or focused individual interviews
    • Use a flexible interview guide covering a specific set of topics
    • Allow the interviewer to change the order and ask follow-up questions when useful
    • Work especially well with busy executives, technical experts, and thought leaders

What Are the Commonly Used Techniques in IDI?

  • Laddering
    • Begin with a concrete product choice or attribute, then work upward step by step
    • Connect the product to its attributes, the attributes to consumer benefits or needs, and those needs to underlying values
    • Example: identifying what drives a consumer’s smartphone choice
      • Which smartphone brand do you use? iPhone.
      • What do you value about it? Its App Store.
      • Why is the App Store important to you? It gives me access to apps that I rely on and cannot find on some other devices.
  • Symbolic analysis
    • Explore an object’s meaning by comparing it with its opposite or imagining its absence
    • Example: understanding the role of a smartphone in the consumer’s life
      • Imagine that you no longer had a smartphone. What would change in your daily life?

What Are the Commonly Used Techniques in IDI?

  • Hidden issue
    • Understand respondents’ feeling about sensitive issues in their lives
    • Ask individuals to construct specific “best case” and “worst case” scenarios so that their daydreams, anxieties and hopes are brought to the surface
    • Examples:
      • What was the happiest time in your life?
      • What would you do with your time if you were given 1 million dollars?

Types of Qualitative Methods: Focus Groups

  • A small number of participants who are led by a moderator have an in-depth discussion about one particular topic or concept
    • Usually consist of 8 to 12 participants
    • Emphasis on group dynamics, interaction, and open discussion
    • A response will generate more from other people in the group
    • Interaction between group members can be observed
    • More in-depth information about consumer preferences or feelings can be obtained

What Are the Key Elements of Focus Groups?

  • Moderator
    • Person hired by the client to lead the group
    • Need excellent communication and organizational skills
  • Discussion guide
    • A written outline of topics to be covered during discussion
  • Focus group length
    • Usually 60–90 minutes
    • More questions → less time to discuss each question
Source: CDC, Using Focus Groups for Evaluation.

What Are the Pros and Cons of Focus Groups?

Pros
  • Getting in-depth information
  • Enables complex issues to be discussed
  • Process highlights differences between consumers
Cons
  • Findings identify themes and explanations, but do not estimate population percentages or prevalence
  • Difficulty in getting attendees
  • Minority viewpoints may not be heard or may be exaggerated
  • Requires a skilled moderator

Types of Qualitative Methods: Projective Techniques

  • When do direct questions fail?
    • The issue is unimportant to respondent
      • Do you prefer the packaging of Colgate or Crest? Kleenex or Puffs?
    • Group norms, social pressures are significant
      • Would you tell your friends that you prefer a budget smartphone to the newest flagship model?
    • Consumer doesn’t want to appear ignorant
      • How useful do you find your phone’s end-to-end encryption settings?
    • Need for privacy
      • Have you been treated for mental illness?
      • Which of the following drugs have you tried?
      • Have you ever cheated on income taxes?
    • Respondent may not be fully aware of their “true” motivation
      • Why did you buy a BMW?

What Are the Different Types of Projective Techniques?

Presentation of an ambiguous, unstructured object, activity, or person that a respondent is asked to interpret and explain.
Categories of Projective Techniques
  • Word Association
  • Completion Test
  • Picture Interpretation
  • Third Person Techniques
  • Role Playing
  • Case Studies
  • Other Projective Techniques like Photo Sort, Pictured Aspirations Technique (PAT), etc.

Types of Projective Techniques: Word Association

  • Researcher gives a word, term, brand-name or product
  • Respondent gives immediately top-of-the-mind thought
  • If the respondent fails to answer within 3 seconds, some emotional involvement with the word is assumed
  • Used to select brand names, advertising campaign themes or slogans
Ex: “What is the first word that comes to mind when you hear Apple?”

Types of Projective Techniques: Completion Test

  • Use in conjunction with word association tests
  • Provides more structure than word association test
  • Respondent is furnished with an incomplete story or group of sentences and asked to complete it
  • Ex: People who ride motorcycles are…
    • Free, independent people who enjoy the outdoors and doing things
    • Scary and are usually criminals or at least some type of gang
    • A lot of times professionals, like lawyers, doctors, and business people, not people you would normally think as being bikers

Types of Projective Techniques: Picture Interpretation

  • Also called Thematic Apperception Test (TAT)
  • Respondents are shown one or more pictures where consumers and products are in the center of attention
  • Subjects asked about what is happening in the pictures
  • Real photos or drawings can be used

Example: Picture Interpretation

  • What is she doing?
  • Where is she?
  • What will she do next?
  • What type of wine is she drinking?
  • What does wine mean to her?

Major Limitations of Qualitative Methods

  • Findings can be misinterpreted because analysis relies on researcher judgment
  • Small samples are not designed to be statistically representative of the population
  • The moderator or interviewer can influence the discussion, responses, and interpretation
